claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability of near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles is governed by a balance between configurational-entropy stabilization and surface-driven diffusion and segregation.
Near-equiatomic multi-element compositions have high configurational entropy.
High configurational entropy favors or stabilizes a random single-phase solid solution over intermetallic formation.
The configurational-entropy stabilization described for HEAs applies to nanoscale near-equiatomic particles under the specified service temperatures.
A higher nanoparticle surface-to-volume ratio increases the relative contribution of surface energy.
Surface-energy contributions accelerate atomic diffusion at elevated temperature.
Thermally activated surface diffusion promotes elemental segregation.
Thermally activated surface diffusion promotes nucleation of ordered, intermetallic, or other secondary phases.
Elemental segregation and secondary-phase formation undermine single-phase stability.
At fixed composition and thermal exposure, smaller nanoparticles have a greater propensity for structural and chemical instability than larger nanoparticles.
Larger nanoparticles retain their single-phase structure longer than smaller nanoparticles under otherwise identical conditions.
Surface-passivating modifications improve retention of the single-phase structure and homogeneous elemental distribution.
Smaller nanoparticles develop detectable phase decomposition or surface-composition gradients earlier than the baseline.
Nanoparticles from the standard synthesis and size distribution may degrade at the highest service temperatures.
Pre-existing phase segregation and strongly stabilizing capping layers or oxide shells can place the material outside the proposed mechanism's domain.
The critical particle size or surface-energy threshold at which surface-driven diffusion overtakes entropy stabilization is not established.
The magnitude and temperature threshold of the proposed size effect depend on the specific alloying elements.
